headlines.title: CTE study on NFL players raises questions about California's youth concussion protocol
headlines.description: There is renewed concern about whether enough is being done to prevent the youth sports concussions following a major study that found at least a quarter of NFL players are expected to develop a degenerative brain disease. “What’s happening when these individuals are younger? How many little hits are they getting that leads to them having CTE? And what can we do at that younger age group to prevent these athletes from getting that?” asked Dr. Nirav Pandya, a pediatric orthopedic surgeon with UCSF Benioff who specializes in sports medicine for young athletes. Concussions in general affect around two million teenagers and children in the U.S. every year, according to the National Center for Health Statistics. Boys tackle football has the highest rate of concussions, according to the CDC, and girls soccer is number two. Girls in general have a higher change of sports-related concussions than boys, the agency said, in part because girls may report more and health care professionals like athletic trainers are less likely to be at girls’ practices and games to identify injuries. California’s student athlete concussion protocol In California, school coaches are required to take an online training course on concussions. If they suspect a concussion, they must remove the student athlete from the game or practice for at least that day until cleared by a licensed health care provider. If a concussion is confirmed, the student must complete a gradual return-to-play protocol lasting at least seven days. California’s student athlete concussion protocol. “I think the tough thing with all of this is that you are basing it on a kid reporting symptoms and someone identifying them,” said Dr. Pandya who said he recently had a patient whose concussions went undiagnosed for over a year. “He had horrible headaches, had problems learning for over a year and had multiple concussions and hadn’t gotten treatment,” Dr. Pandya said. “A concussion, there’s no MRI; no blood test for it.” Reporter Candice Nguyen (left) and Dr. Nirav Pandya (right). Ben Nguyen’s concussion story Earlier this year, Ben Nguyen, a senior at Archbishop Mitty High School in San Jose, California, says he suffered a serious concussion during a wrestling match. “I felt incredibly nauseous,” he recalled. Nguyen shared cell phone video of the moment he got concussed. It showed his opponent go in for a takedown when Nguyen responds by trying to flip the other student over his own body. Image from video shared by Ben Nguyen. “His should and neck were kind of in my chin area,” he said. “The impact kind of went straight to my head.” The impact wasn’t obvious, but the symptoms afterward were. “I couldn’t think as fast anymore…I was like throwing up in the bus ride. I was throwing up right after my match as well,” Nguyen said. Nguyen said he felt a little nervous about telling his coach and athletic trainer, who’s a sports health care professional on the team. Ben Nguyen, Archbishop Mitty High School wrestler. “The impact looked so subtle. I was kind of scared of them being like, ‘Oh, there’s nothing, you can go back,’” Nguyen said. He said that didn’t happen and his school took his injury seriously. However, he admits, it’s easy for students to get around the concussion protocols if they want. “I have a friend in football who had all the hallmark symptoms of concussions, he just lied on the survey to get back into practice,” he said. NBC Bay Area reached out to Archbishop Mitty High School. The school declined to participate in this story. The California Interscholastic Federation, which established the state’s student athlete concussion protocol, said it’s important for everyone involved to make sure the return-to-play process is followed. The solutions, the science, and the debate “If we can empower kids to understand that it’s okay to speak up. Number two, the system, athletic trainers, physical therapists, anyone who’s looking over these kids.Then, I think there are more drastic things that we talk about like, how can we decrease the number of chances or times that someone can get hit? Maybe that means delaying when kids start playing tackle football,” Dr. Pandya said. It’s some of those drastic suggestions that continue to get pushback. “My big concern is when we hear results about people who play the most elite level, that there’s a reaction of looking at, well, what do we do at the youth level? And these are very different games,” said David Camarillo who is Associate Professor of Bioengineering, (by courtesy) Mechanical Engineering and Neurosurgery at Stanford University. Camarillo has been studying concussions for the past 15 years testing thousands of helmets in his lab, CamLab, in Stanford. CamLab at Stanford University. The results he’s talking about come from a recent study published in the British Medical Journal showing at least a quarter of NFL players will likely develop a neurodegenerative disease like CTE. The NFL said it’s aware of the study, and it’s ensuring its community has access to expanding resources. Camarillo believes the science points to urgent action needed at the professional level. “Does it mean kids shouldn’t play sports? I don’t think we have enough information to say yes to that,” Camarillo said. David Camarillo, Assoc. Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. When asked what’s the harm in taking preventative action in case certain youth sports are connected to developing CTE later in life, Camarillo said he believes taking action at an individual level is perfectly fair. “I think it’s a very different thing to make a law, to make public policy that affects everybody, that takes away a right to choose. That ought to have scientific evidence behind it,” he added. Why isn’t there evidence? The British Medical Journal study relied on hundreds of NFL players donating their brains to science after they die. We don’t have that kind of data on our young athletes today. The Investigative Unit spoke to numerous doctors, researchers, and students about this issue over the past several weeks. All said the best solution right now is education and schools fostering a culture where students feel encouraged to report concussion symptoms. “If it wasn’t for like my prior knowledge or like my friends or like me witnessing it first-hand, I probably would have lied to get back into wrestling,” Nguyen said. Candice Nguyen is the senior investigative reporter on this story. If you have a question about this story or a story tip, email her at candice.nguyen@nbcuni.com.

headlines.title: Neighbors frustrated after vandals target more San Jose schools
headlines.description: The list of South Bay schools hit by vandals continues to grow. Meyer Elementary School in San Jose is the latest campus targeted by vandals, who pulled and cut copper and electrical wire from underground cement boxes and panels. Windows were also smashed and the multipurpose room was ransacked. “Super sad because I went to school here and my kids went to school here,” said Dara Cano, who lives across the streety from Meyer Elementary School. Cano said her neighborhood is tired of seeing old school sites vandalized. Meyer was one of eight schools the Alum Rock Union Elementary School District closed last year. The district said six of those campuses remain vacant. Joseph George Middle School is one of the vacant campuses vandalized. The shuttered school was recently vandalized for a second time since closing, causing an estimated $200,000 in damage for the cash-strapped school district. The district is planning to discuss the vandalism at a special board meeting Thursday and frustrated neighbors are hopeful action will be taken to protect the schools. San Jose Oct 13 San Jose Oct 14 San Jose Oct 13

headlines.title: Los Gatos' ‘Fantasy of Lights' is walk-through only with fewer days this year
headlines.description: Big changes are in store this year for one of the South Bay’s biggest holiday attractions. Fantasy of Lights in Los Gatos will be cutting back the number of days it’s open significantly and switching from a mostly drive-through to an entirely walking format, the county confirmed. The county also noted that rising costs played a role in these changes. Fantasy of Lights is a county-run holiday light display that has been in existence since 1999. The event used to be exclusively a drive-through, where families would pack into their cars and drive through the 1.5-mile route at Vasona Lake County Park. But in recent years, organizers have added a couple of days when guests could walk the route. This year, the county confirms the event will be an only walk-through event. “We did not make this decision lightly,” said Audrey Ann Díaz, Acting Senior Communications Officer for Santa Clara County. “Like many beloved community traditions, Fantasy of Lights has faced rising operational costs over the years,” Díaz explained. She also noted that the walk-through events in the past have been “wildly successful,” complete with a drone show, live entertainment, and more food options. The event will also only run for four days this year from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m.: Saturday, Dec. 5 Sunday, Dec. 6 Saturday, Dec. 12 Sunday, Dec. 13 This new schedule is substantially shorter. In the past, the event has been for several walk-through-only days, followed by more than two weeks of drive-through days. It will be a noticeable change for families used to driving through the attraction, instead of paying for tickets per car, each person will need to purchase a ticket (tickets for those ages 13 and up are $25, tickets for youth ages 4-12 are $10, and tickets for children 3 and under are free). Tickets must be purchased in advance.

headlines.title: Oakland police tout drop in crime, but chief pushes for more progress
headlines.description: Oakland police on Thursday said crime is down across all major categories, but the chief acknowledged there’s still work to do. Chief James Beere said homicides this year are down more than 20% compared to the same period last year. Robberies and burglaries are down 26%. Beere said more needs to be done to address increases in larceny and robberies involving weapons. “I want to acknowledge something that’s very important. For those of us who have been victims of crime, these statistics may not reflect how you feel and how safe you feel,” Beere said. “We understand that and we take these concerns very seriously. At the same time, many of our residents have told us that they feel much safer.” Beere credited the decline in crime to collaboration between the community, city leadership and law enforcement partners. Beere acknowledged staffing remains a challenge. The police department currently has 601 officers. Beere pointed to a recent audit that found the department needs at least 877 officers to maintain its current level of service. Oakland 15 hours ago Oakland 18 hours ago

headlines.title: Bay Area company's air taxi in final stages of testing with FAA
headlines.description: A Bay Area company is testing new technology that could one day have people flying over the streets instead of driving on them. San Jose-based Archer Aviation has created an electric air taxi, and the company was out in Oakland Thursday performing test flights. “This beautiful aircraft is an air taxi that’s under development at the company,” Archer Aviation Chief Strategy Officer Eric Lentell said. “We’re going through kind of the final stages of testing with the FAA to be able to bring it to market.” The goal is to defeat traffic congestion in cities, while being competitive with Uber Black or Uber Premiere pricing. “Really focused on kind of 10- to 20-mile routes where it takes about 60 to 90 minutes in a car and we can do in about 10 minutes,” Lentell said. An air taxi seats four people, plus a pilot. The technology is similar to an electric car but in an aircraft. The company has focused on both conventional and vertical takeoffs and landings. “The big change, the big step change is distributed electric propulsion,” Lentell said. “With going all electric on an aircraft instead of a typical combustion engine, you can rethink the design of these aircraft.”

headlines.title: Trump administration sues California to block state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots
headlines.description: The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month’s midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department said California officials failed to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. The lawsuit follows a letter sent earlier this week by a top Justice Department official who threatened potential legal action if California didn’t comply. The federal government didn’t specify where the 20,000 voters were concentrated, but the list was sent directly to Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan on Tuesday, his office confirmed in a statement. His office said the list contained names of voters throughout California, not just Los Angeles, even though Logan is the only county election official named as a defendant in the lawsuit. He doesn’t have jurisdiction over ballots outside Los Angeles County. In a statement Thursday, Logan said his office can’t withhold ballots or refuse to count them “based solely on unverified allegations.” Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and there are a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts that could determine which party has control of the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. Expert says lawsuit could set stage for false election claims California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a letter to the Justice Department that the federal government hasn’t provided evidence to support its allegation that 20,000 names on the state’s voter rolls are of noncitizens. She referenced an instance in which the federal government initially alleged nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens were listed on Nevada’s voter rolls, but the state determined that all the people flagged were, in fact, U.S. citizens. She also noted that voting is already underway in the state. Weber, a Democrat, said the Justice Department was “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.” California’s elections are in “full compliance” with federal law, she added. David Becker, an election law expert who heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research, called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “fairly frivolous.” “If they were seeking to work in good faith to clean up the voter list that they believed had issues, they would have done this months ago in a much different fashion,” Becker said. “However, it does raise questions as to whether or not the sole purpose of this is to set the stage for false claims about elections.” List of alleged illegal voters delivered on a thumb drive Logan said his office received the thumb drive along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.” Becker said most election officials’ cybersecurity protocols would not allow them to comply with the Justice Department’s request as it was sent. “Election offices do not just stick thumb drives into their technology, for very good reason,” he said. The Justice Department’s lawsuit says the federal government sought to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and “California made no serious effort to do so.” “The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question,” the lawsuit says. “This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined.” Weber, who is named in the lawsuit, suggested the federal government’s outreach had not been collaborative. She said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them. In her letter Thursday, she called the recent demands “an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.” Letters sent weeks before elections The letter sent by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave the state 48 hours to research the list of the 20,000 people it claims might not be citizens. For those whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their immigration status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at an unrelated press conference Thursday morning that state officials would not carry out the federal government’s requests to withhold ballots for the alleged noncitizen voters. He noted that the administration’s alleged number of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls had dropped from the 190,000 flagged over the summer by the Department of Homeland Security to the 20,000 noted by the Justice Department. “What happened to those 170,000? They just got those wrong,” Bonta said. He also said the Trump administration was violating a federal law that prohibits states from changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election. “They are in unprecedented, baseless, lawless territory,” he said. The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, defended the Justice Department’s move to take California to court. “This is not political or controversial,” he wrote in a post on X. “We will not allow California to dilute the votes of American citizens.” ___ Austin reported from Sacramento, Riddle from Los Angeles and Durkin Richer from Washington. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed. .
headlines.source: Alanna Durkin Richer | The Associated Press, Sophie Austin | The Associated Press and Safiyah Riddle | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Lanes of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco to close this weekend
headlines.description: All southbound lanes and one northbound lane of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco will be closed this weekend for an ongoing construction project. The closure between Cesar Chavez Street and 17th Street will start at 11 p.m. Friday and continue until 6 a.m. Monday, according to Caltrans. Motorists should avoid the area and consider taking Interstate 280 as an alternate, Caltrans said. The closure will affect drivers heading out of San Francisco on the Central Freeway and those driving into San Francisco from the East Bay over the Bay Bridge, hoping through the city on highway 101. It will also affect those heading to Chase Center for the Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. This marks the third closure for the ongoing Hospital Curve repaving and rehabilitation project, which started last fall. The fourth and final closure – impacting the same lanes as this weekend’s closure – is scheduled for the weekend of Nov. 6-9, weather permitting, according to Caltrans.

headlines.title: Elderly woman seriously injured in San Francisco hit and run involving e-bike
headlines.description: A hit-and-run collision involving an electric bicycle seriously injured an 88-year-old woman on Upper Market Street in San Francisco on Wednesday evening, according to police. The collision was reported at about 5:30 p.m. in the area of Market and Church streets. San Francisco police said the woman was crossing the street when a bicyclist hit her and then fled the scene. The woman was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries and an update on her condition was not immediately available Thursday. No arrest has been made in the case and police have not shared any details about the suspect or bicycle. Anyone with information about the collision is asked to call the SFPD tip line at 415-575-4444 or to send a tip by text message to TIP411 with “SFPD” at the start of the message.

headlines.title: Bay Area features in top 10 of WalletHub's greenest cities in America
headlines.description: Multiple cities in the Bay Area and Northern California were named in WalletHub’s 2026 Greenest Cities in America list. Oakland, San Jose and San Francisco were the top three cities on the list, respectively, while Fremont was placed seventh. WalletHub’s ranking was composed of 100 cities in the U.S. compared on metrics of environment, transportation, energy sources, and lifestyle and policy. Oakland has the second-lowest greenhouse gas emissions and the best air quality in the country, alongside the lowest light pollution levels in the country. The city also has the 30th-highest percentage of designated parkland among the 100 cities in WalletHub’s list with 12%. In addition, Oakland has the 20th-most bicycle lanes and paths, a high number of community garden sites and farmers’ markets, and ranked 24th in most green job openings per capita. San Jose boasts the fifth-highest number of solar panel installations per capita and the fifth-highest percentage of electricity coming from renewable sources at 50%. San Jose also has the fourth-lowest Urban Heat Island Effect Index in the country, with the use of green energy in the city helping to keep it from being an excessively hot environment. San Jose also bans plastic bags, has a bike-sharing program and employs many initiatives that promote the use of green energy. San Francisco’s approach to locally sourced food helped it reach top three in WalletHub’s list. It leads the country in Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) groups and community garden sites per capita. It also has the fourth-most farmers’ markets per capita. Like San Jose, San Francisco gets more than 50% of its energy from renewable sources, the fifth-highest percentage in the country. Residents’ water conservation efforts placed San Francisco at the ninth-lowest daily water consumption per capita in the country. San Francisco also has the 13th-most alternative-fuel stations for vehicles and the 20th-most solar panel installations per capita. The city is also ranked fourth in transportation for the low percentage of commuters who drive to work by themselves. While Fremont was seventh overall, the city was joint-ranked first for environment and energy sources. The city issued a statement saying the ranking was the result of a strong commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, preserving ample green space and advancements in renewable energy. Stockton was ranked 27th in WalletHub’s 100 greenest cities list and joint-first in energy sources.

headlines.title: Average long-term US mortgage rate holds at 7.4%, remaining at highest level in nearly 3 years
headlines.description: Mortgage rates held steady this week, keeping the average long-term U.S. home loan rate at its highest level in nearly three years. The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was unchanged from last week at 7.40%, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.27%. The latest reading ends a seven-week climb for the average rate, which is at the highest level since Nov. 16, 2023, when it was at 7.44%. Meanwhile, borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, eased this week. That average rate dropped to 6.71% from 6.73% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.52%. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. Mortgage rates have been climbing since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher. The run-up in rates also reflects heightened bond market volatility, which has pushed up yields on U.S. Treasurys. U.S. home sales remain stalled this year in large part because of rising mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power and prompting many to put off buying a home. The recent string of mortgage rate increases snapped as the 10-year Treasury yield pulled back from its highest level since 2002. The yield was at 5.10% at midday Thursday on the bond market. It had topped 5.30% earlier this month amid worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. It’s still well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran began. In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. The 1.42 percentage point increase in the rate since then translates roughly into an additional monthly cost of $376 for a borrower financing a $400,000 home loan at the current average rate. Depending on a borrower’s income, credit and other factors, they may qualify for a rate on a 30-year mortgage that is below or above the current average. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. This week, the National Association of Realtors said that existing U.S. home sales rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year earlier amid rising mortgage rates and home prices. The surge in mortgage rates in recent weeks has put off many would-be homebuyers. Mortgage applications, which include loans to buy a home or refinance an existing mortgage, fell 2.7% last week from the previous week as mortgage rates rose, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Faced with higher borrowing costs due to rising mortgage rates, more homebuyers are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs. Such loans, which typically offer lower initial interest rates than traditional 30-year, fixed-rate mortgages, accounted for 10.5% of all mortgage applications last week — the highest level in a year, MBA said. Despite holding steady this week, it’s likely that the recent upward march in mortgage rates is not over. Reports this week showing prices at the consumer and wholesale level rose more than economists expected flashed the latest sign that inflation has worsened as rising oil prices add on costs to all manner of goods and services. The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate by December, and could set the stage for more rate increases early next year, said Jiayi Xu, a senior economist at Realtor.com. “In other words, mortgage rates are unlikely to ease anytime soon, but bringing inflation under control would pave the way for lower rates and a much-needed boost to affordability for the year ahead,” Xu said. Wall Street traders now expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at its next policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase in December have jumped to 64.6% from 49.9% a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. While the central bank doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately affect the yield on 10-year Treasurys. In its latest forecast, mortgage buyer Fannie Mae projects that the rate on a 30-year mortgage will average 7.4% in the final quarter of this year and average 7.5% in 2027.

headlines.title: Preliminary 2.5 magnitude earthquake strikes near Gilroy
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.5 magnitude earthquake struck near Gilroy late Thursday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 10:57 a.m. and was centered 6.1 miles east-southeast of Gilroy, 9.9 miles north-northwest of Hollister and 14.5 miles southeast of Morgan Hill, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Testimony begins in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: Testimony began on Thursday in the federal corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao. Leigh Hanson, Thao’s former chief of staff in 2023, testified about the oversized role Thao’s longtime boyfriend and co-defendant, Andre Jones, had in her administration despite not being a city employee. Hanson said Jones appeared uninvited on a Zoom interview for an important role in the administration. Hanson also testified that Jones threatened her job as chief of staff after she walked out of a meeting with Jones, the mayor and the city attorney because she believed Jones’ presence as a non-employee would jeopardize attorney-client privilege. Jones allegedly told Hanson afterward, “We’ll see which one is left at the end of the day.” Hanson was fired by Thao’s interim successor after Thao was recalled. Sheng Thao Oct 13 Sheng Thao Oct 13 Sheng Thao Oct 14 Sheng Thao Jul 30 Federal prosecutors have indicted Thao on charges of bribery, conspiracy and wire fraud, along with Jones and David and Andy Duong. The Duongs own California Waste Solutions, Oakland’s recycling contractor. Federal prosecutors allege Thao helped the company secure future contracts with the city of Oakland in exchange for helping her get elected mayor and payments to Jones. Thao and her co-defendants have pleaded not guilty to all charges. Hanson also testified about Thao overruling her and hiring Larry Gallegos as deputy director of housing, even though Hanson did not believe Gallegos was the right fit. Prosecutors allege Thao would use Gallegos to have the city buy 100 housing units from Evolutionary Homes, one of the companies at the center of the alleged bribery scheme involving the Duongs. Thursday marks the first day of testimony in the corruption trial, with Hanson the first of 68 potential witnesses federal prosecutors could call.
headlines.source: Bob Redell and Jaxon Van Derbeken
